12. Mr. Zakir Hossain Bhuiyan further submits that the defendants miserably failed to prove that the suit land vested in the Government as khas land during the S. A. operation, in view of the fact that neither they adduced any minimum iota of evidence including the khas khatian itself before the courts below in support of their contention nor did they disclose the source through which or what basis or the manner in which the suit land devolved upon the Government and as such the plea of khas khatian which is the genesis of the defendants' case falls flat and therefore, the suit was rightly decreed by the trial Court. In this connection Mr. Bhuiyan drew the attention to Section 92 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and referred to the decisions of Geeta Rani alais Shamima Khatun vs. Bangladesh, 36 DLR (AD) 225; Bangladesh and others vs. Mallick Ali Ahmed and others, 3CLR (AD) 345; and Md. Kalam Mollah and others vs. Sheikh Samsu and others, 23 BLT 320, which will be discussed later on. 

 22. On the other hand, Mr. Shah Hossain the learned Advocate for the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 submits that on and from 14th April, 1956 the rent receiving interest of all the rent receivers in Bangladesh having been acquired by the Government under Section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (the SAT Act), the plaintiff-petitioners claim of title to the suit land on the strength of a compromise decree dated 26.02.1957 drawn up in Rent Suit No. 60 of 1957 between the then Zaminder/landlord Satish Chandra Das and his tenants Mohammad Mozahar Ali Miah and Azhar Ali Miah from whom the petitioners got the suit land by way of successive transfers becomes barred by law. In support of his submission, Mr. Hossain referred to the decisions reported in 31 DLR (AD) 323; 14 BLC 848; 38 DLR (AD) 93; and 20 DLR 699.  30. It is the case of the defendant-opposite parties that the suit land vested in the Government as khas land during the S. A. operation, but none of them adduced any evidence including the khas khatian itself before the courts below in support of their contention. Again, although the Government filed a written statement, they did not adduce any evidence, oral or documentary, to show as to when, why and how the suit land became khas in their name and as such the written statement of the Government will not ipso facto be admissible in evidence unless and until the same is supported by competent witnesses of convincing nature, and as such Section 92 of the SAT Act as well as the decisions referred to by the plaintiff-petitioner will stand in the way of the claim of defendants.
